The '''Hang''' ({{IPA|de|haŋ}};<ref>{{cite book | title=Duden Aussprachewörterbuch | edition=6| year=2006 | publisher=Bibliographisches Institut & F.A. Brockhaus AG | location=Mannheim}}</ref> plural form: Hanghang)<ref>[http://www.hangblog.org/panart/Booklet_englisch_GzD1.pdf PANArt Hang Bookl008] p. 8</ref> is a type of [[musical instrument]] fitting into the [[Idiophone|idiophone class]] and based on the Trinidad & Tobago [[steelpan]]. It was created by Felix Rohner and Sabina Schärer in [[Bern]], Switzerland, and marketed by their company, PANArt Hangbau AGa. They took the name "Hang" from a [[Bernese German]] word that means both "hand" and "hillside". Though it has sometimes been referred to as a "Hang drum", the inventors consider this a [[misnomer]].

The Hang is constructed from two half-shells of [[Deep drawing|deep-drawn]], [[Nitriding|nitrided]] steel sheet glued together at the rim, leaving the inside hollow and creating the shape of a [[convex lens]]. The top ("Ding") side has a center 'note' hammered into it and seven or eight 'tone fields' hammered around the center. The bottom ("Gu") is a plain surface that has a rolled hole in the center with a tuned note that can be created when the rim is struck. The instrument uses some of the same basic physical principles as a steelpan, but modified in such a way as to act as a [[Helmholtz resonator]].

The Hang has gone through several iterations, and since its manufacture was discontinued in 2013, PANArt has continued to develop other musical instruments. Global interest in the Hang has led to the creation of similar instruments that are referred to as [[handpan]]s.

==Creation and development==
[[File:Hangfamily.jpg|thumb|right|Front line: Prototype Hang from November 1999 (left), Ghatam (right); second line: Three Hanghang, built in 2007, 2006, and 2005, respectively (from left to right)]]

The Hang was developed in 2000 by Felix Rohner and Sabina Schärer in [[Bern]], Switzerland, and introduced at the [[Frankfurt Trade Fair]] in 2001. The pair, who had spent many years developing it,<ref name="PANArt Hang Booklet 2008">[http://www.hangblog.org/panart/Booklet_englisch_GzD1.pdf PANArt Hang Booklet 2008] pp. 4ff</ref> subsequently formed the company PANArt Hangbau AG, under which the instrument would be marketed.<ref>David Wessel, Andrew Morrison, Thomas Rossing: ''Sound of the Hang''. Paper for the 155. Meeting of the Acoustical Society of America, Paris 2008, pp. 6257–6262 ([http://webistem.com/acoustics2008/acoustics2008/cd1/data/articles/002762.pdf PDF file; 1,5 MB]).</ref> They adopted the name from a [[Bernese German]] word that has a double meaning, one of which is "hand" and the other "hillside",<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sylvainpasliermusic.com/single-post/the-origins-of-handpans-the-panart-hang|title=The Origins of Handpans: The Hang from PANArt {{!}} Sylvain Paslier – Handpan Artist|website=Sylvain Paslier – Handpan Artist|access-date=7 November 2018}}</ref> referring to its [[Convex lens|convex]] shape. It is a registered [[trademark]] and property of PANArt.<ref>''[http://www.wipo.int/branddb/en/showData.jsp?ID=MAD.0969295 WIPO Global Brand Database].'' International Registration Number 969295</ref> Over time, it came to be called a "Hang drum", but Rohner and Schärer have discouraged this, as they consider it a [[misnomer]].<ref name="letter2009">{{Cite web|url=http://www.hangblog.org/letter-from-the-hangbauhaus-november-2009/|title=Letter from the Hangbauhaus November 2009 |website=Hangblog.org|access-date=19 April 2021}}</ref>

The Hang is a type of [[handpan]], fitting into the [[Idiophone|idiophone class]] and based on the Trinidad & Tobago [[steelpan]]. It is {{cvt|52|cm|0}} in diameter and has a height of {{cvt|24|cm|0}}. The two [[Deep drawing|deep-drawn]] steel hemispheres are hardened by a process known as gas [[nitridization]].<ref>Felix Rohner, Sabina Schärer: [http://www.hangblog.org/panart/Paper-Hang-2007.pdf History, Development and Tuning of the Hang]. pp. 1f</ref><ref>Lukas Vogelsang: ''Die Welt ist Blech. Über einen neu gefundenen Klang.'' In: ''ensuite – kulturmagazin.'' Bern, issue no. 4, April 2004, pp. 4–5 ([http://www.ensuite.ch/pdfs/ausgaben04/ensuite_4_04.pdf PDF file; 2,8 MB]). (German)</ref> The side considered the bottom has an opening ("Gu") in the center, which allows the generation of a [[bass note]] through [[Helmholtz Resonator|Helmholtz]] resonance.<ref name="Physics Today">{{cite journal |title=The extraordinary sound of the hang |first1=Andrew |last1=Morrison |first2=Thomas D. |last2=Rossing |journal=Physics Today |date=March 2009 |volume=62 |issue=3 |page=66 |doi= 10.1063/1.3099586 |bibcode=2009PhT....62c..66M |doi-access=free }}</ref> When it is played in a damped way, it can change in pitch similar to a [[talking drum]]. On the top are seven or eight notes arranged in a tone circle in zigzag fashion, from low to high. All are tuned harmonically (with [[Fundamental frequency|fundamental]], [[octave]], and the [[Perfect fifth|fifth]] above the octave) around a low note ("Ding") at the center of the tone circle. Each unit is numbered and signed.<ref>{{Cite web|url= http://newindianexpress.com/magazine/article303182.ece|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160304122053/http://www.newindianexpress.com/magazine/article303182.ece|url-status= dead|archive-date= 4 March 2016|title=Bewitching musical hearts across the world|work=The New Indian Express|access-date=20 September 2010}}</ref>

===First generation===
From 2001 to 2005, the first-generation Hang was offered in multiple scales ranging up to 45 different sound models. Its creators took their initial inspiration from [[ethnomusicological]] roots, with notes and scales such as the [[Aeolian mode|Aeolian]], [[Akebono scale|Akebono]], [[Arabic maqam#Ajnas|Hijaz]], and [[Pygmy music]].<ref>Michael Paschko: ''[http://www.hangblog.org/hang-sound-models/ Hang Sound Models]''.</ref> From 2001 to 2004, each Hang had eight tone fields in the circle. In 2005, PANArt was able to lower the tones on the Hang significantly in what they referred to as the "Low Hang", with the Ding tuned to F<sub>3</sub>, E<sub>3</sub>, or E{{music|b}}<sub>3</sub>. It was offered in two versions, with eight or seven tone fields in the circle. Each unit was numbered, the name of the sound model was written, and a signature of either Felix Rohner or Sabina Schärer was pasted on the inside of the Ding surface.

===Second generation===
[[File:Panart hang 5stages en.jpg|thumb|400px|Five development stages of the PANArt Hang]]

In 2006, a new generation of Hang was introduced. It had a surface coating of [[Annealing (metallurgy)|annealed]] brass over the nitrided steel as well as a ring of brass around the circumference. The Ding had a central note at D<sub>3</sub> and two A notes (A<sub>3</sub> and A<sub>4</sub>) as well as another D (D<sub>4</sub>) in the tone circle.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hangblog.org/letter-from-hangbauhaus-bern-end-of-march-2007/|title=Letter from Hangbauhaus – Bern, End of March, 2007 |website=Hangblog.org|access-date=19 April 2021}}</ref> The remaining notes were mixed into several different configurations. The majority of second-generation Hanghang were built with seven tone fields in the circle. Older Hanghang had tone fields with the oval indentation oriented radially towards the Ding, whereas the 2007 models (as well as the Integral Hang) had tone fields angled at about 45° from a line drawn from the Ding to the edge.

===Integral Hang===
In 2008, a new version of the instrument was announced, named the Integral Hang, which included several modifications. It had only one scale, with seven tone fields in the cycle (D<sub>3</sub> Ding, A<sub>3</sub>, B{{music|b}}<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>4</sub>, D<sub>4</sub>, E<sub>4</sub>, F<sub>4</sub>, A<sub>4</sub>) and no other sound models offered. The Gu hole was adjusted to a subtly oval shape to improve the tuning of the three partials D<sub>5</sub>, F<sub>5</sub>, and an F{{music|#}}<sub>5</sub> on the Gu neck. Significant changes were made to the Ding (center note on the top). A circular indentation in the dome was made and had a texture of annealed and lacquered brass. Additional changes were made to the shoulder area, between the flattened Ding and the notes in the tone circle, making for more gradual transitions than in the previous generation. The PANArt logo, serial number, date of finalization, and signatures of the Hang makers were placed on the Gu side, near the equator, where the two shells meet.<ref>Michael Paschko: ''[http://www.lex.hangblog.org/de/ Das Hanglexikon]''. Keywords: Integrales Hang, Gu, Ding, Seriennummer and Signatur (German)</ref>

By developing the Integral Hang, Rohner and Schärer distanced themselves from the idea of building an instrument for the needs of professional musicians.<ref>Felix Rohner, Sabina Schärer: ''[http://www.hangblog.org/the-integral-hang-2009/ The Integral Hang 2009].''</ref> Their aims and ambitions were published in a "Letter from the Hangbauhaus": {{blockquote
| Our concepts, developments and implementations are far from the musical norms of modern times that require study, practice and performance. Playing with this Hang can lead to a form of freedom, an intimate conversation that can only unfold without pressure and coercion. If individuals are aware of this concept, they will be strengthened by this Hang. Thoughtless use can weaken a person.<ref name="letter2009" />
}}

===Free Integral Hang===
2010 saw the introduction of the Free Integral Hang, which features a few construction changes. The brass ring around the seam connecting the Ding and Gu shells was removed. Furthermore, the dome of the Ding was no longer brass-coated and was characterized by a double offset (a triple dome).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hangblog.org/das-freie-integrale-hang-im-bild/|title=Das Freie Integrale Hang im Bild |website=Hangblog.org|access-date=19 April 2021 |language=de |trans-title=The Free Integral Hang in the picture}}</ref> The Free Integral Hanghang are tuned without the use of [[Electronic tuner|tuning devices]]. The pitch of the Ding differed from one instrument to another, and varied around the tone D<sub>3</sub>. The tones in the tone circle relative to the Ding corresponded to those of the Integral Hang.<ref>Michael Paschko: ''Das Hanglexikon''. Keyword: [http://www.lex.hangblog.org/de/freies-integrales-hang.htm Freies Integrales Hang] (German)</ref>

==Termination of Hang manufacturing and development of new Pang instruments==
As of December 2013, PANArt announced<ref>PANArt Hang Manufacturing Ltd.: [http://www.gubal.ch/en/news/category/news-hang News: Hang] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220819022945/http://www.gubal.ch/en/news/category/news-hang |date=19 August 2022 }} (17 December 2013) Accessed 25 April 2015</ref> that the Hang would no longer be made, as its makers were shifting to the creation of a new instrument, the [[Gubal (instrument)|Gubal]].<ref>PANArt Hang Manufacturing Ltd.: [http://panart.ch/en/articles/from-the-hang-to-the-gubal From the Hang to the Gubal]</ref> In the following years, PANArt developed a number of other instruments, such as the Hang Gudu, Hang Urgu, Hang Bal, and Hang Gede. They also created a number of string instruments, together with a collective improvised music form played with these "Pang instruments".<ref>PANArt Hang Manufacturing Ltd.: [http://panart.ch/en/instruments Instruments]</ref><ref>PANArt Hang Manufacturing Ltd.: [http://panart.ch/en/articles/pang-music-the-new-art-form-from-panart Pang music – the new art form from PANArt]</ref>

==Playing==
{{Multiple issues|section=yes|
{{More citations needed section|date=October 2025}}
{{Technical|section|date=October 2025}}
}}
[[File:005 dkg-made detail.jpg|thumb|[[Manu Delago]] playing a first-generation Hang]]

The Hang is typically played resting on the player's lap, using hands and fingers instead of [[Percussion mallet|mallets]]. This lighter means of playing produces a softer and warmer sound than the bright sound of a mallet-based traditional [[steelpan]].

The top ("Ding") side of the Hang, depending on how it is played, can sound like a [[harp]], bells, or harmonically tuned steelpans. The notes are laid out in a cross pattern in the tone circle from low to high, so that with a specific orientation of the Hang, the player can ascend or descend the scale by alternating using the left and right hands to strike the tone fields. Each tone field has multiple overtones oriented specifically in the flattened field with a dome at the center. Typically, there is a [[fundamental tone]], an [[overtone]] tuned to an [[octave]] above that fundamental, and an additional overtone a [[perfect fifth]] above that octave ([[Interval (music)|twelfth or tritave]]). The orientation is fairly consistent across the fields on each Hang, so that the overtones can be highlighted, muted, or extracted based on how and where the player strikes the tone field.

The bottom side of the Hang has a round opening, the "Gu", producing together with the air in the cavity a [[Helmholtz resonance]] similar to a [[ghatam]] or an [[udu]]. In the second generation, known as the Integral Hang and the Free Integral Hang, adjustment of the size of the Gu (by partially blocking it with either a hand or the legs) can generate a sympathetic D<sub>2</sub> from the Helmholtz resonance, which introduces subtle layers of cross-complexities in the resonance of the instrument as notes are played on the "Ding" side. In the first- and second-generation models, there is a single high note with a long sustain that can be generated by striking the rim of the hole on the "Gu" side. On the Integral Hang, there are two notes that can be generated (F and F{{music|#}}). The Hang can also be used as a [[friction idiophone]]. [[Shaker (musical instrument)|Shaker]]-like sounds can be made by sliding a hand across the surface, and it can also ring like a [[singing bowl]] by using skin (a hand) or a bow.

In the tuning of a Hang, the focus is not about the precise mathematical frequency ratios of the [[Harmonic series (music)#Partial|partials]] of a tone field but on the impact of the entire sound.<ref>Felix Rohner, Sabina Schärer: ''[http://www.hangblog.org/the-call-of-iron/ The call of iron].''</ref>

==Copyright issues==
PANart, the creators of the Hang, have launched extensive legal proceedings against many handpan builders, deeming their instruments a violation of the company's copyright. In 2025, the [[Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland]] confirmed the preliminary judgment of the Commercial Court of the Canton of Bern that the Hang was subject to copyright as a work of applied art,<ref>Decision [http://relevancy.bger.ch/php/aza/http/index.php?highlight_docid=aza%3A%2F%2F18-02-2025-4A_466-2024&lang=de&type=show_document 4A_466/2024] of 18. Februar 2025</ref> and in 2026, the commercial court found that 210 of the 260 types of handpan submitted to the court violated PANart's copyright. Only models with significant differences, such as instruments whose dome on the top was replaced by a concave tone field, or with triangular rather than circular sound fields, were found not to be in violation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=3 July 2026 |title=Berner Urheberrechtsstreit: 80 Prozent der Handpans verletzen das Recht am Hang |url=https://www.bernerzeitung.ch/handpan-urteil-80-prozent-verletzen-urheberrecht-des-hang-984206505959 |access-date=3 July 2026 |website=Der Bund |language=de |trans-title=Bernese copyright dispute: 80 percent of handpans infringe the rights in the Hang.}}</ref>
